questions.topic: How a revoked status reaches a client
questions.learningObjective: Identify how a revocation answer reaches a validating client
questions.stem: The observatory dome controller presents a certificate that was revoked an hour ago. What must the validating client do to learn of that revocation?

options.text: Query a status responder that holds authoritative revocation data and verify the responder signature on the reply.
Wait for the certificate expiry date to pass before it accepts any new connection from the dome.
options.misconception: believes revocation only matters at expiry time

options.text: Look for the revoked certificate in the issuer published certificate list and treat absence as proof.
options.misconception: confuses a certificate list with a revocation list

options.text: Ask the dome key owner whether it would like to revoke the certificate again this season.
options.misconception: treats the key owner opinion as the revocation source

questions.explanation: Revocation needs an active lookup: ask a responder for current status and verify the response signature. Expiry, a certificate list, or the key owner opinion never gives a reliable answer.
questions.hint: Ask what the client checks while validating.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The freshness a revocation answer needs
questions.learningObjective: Compute how long a client waits before it learns a published revocation
questions.stem: Revocation log: three clients poll a status responder. Client A polls every 60 seconds, client B every 300 seconds, client C every 900 seconds. A revocation is published at 09:00:07 and none of them polled between 09:00:00 and 09:00:07. How many seconds later does client C learn of the revocation?

options.text: 60 seconds, because the fastest poller in the group always learns about a revocation first.
options.misconception: assumes the fastest poller is the one being asked about

options.text: 300 seconds, because client B polls on the middle interval of the three listed clients.
options.misconception: picks the middle value without following the poll cycle

options.text: 893 seconds, because client C next polls fifteen minutes after its nine o clock check.
907 seconds, because the responder own seven second lag is added to the polling interval.
options.misconception: adds the responder lag to the polling interval

questions.explanation: Client C polls every 900 seconds and last checked at 09:00:00, so its next check is 09:15:00, which is 893 seconds after publication. The faster pollers do not change when client C is told.
questions.hint: Work out the next poll time, then count the gap.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What boundary a hardware module draws
questions.learningObjective: Explain the boundary a hardware security module draws around key material
questions.stem: Explain what boundary a hardware security module draws when an observatory keeps its long term signing key inside the module.

answer.exemplar: The module keeps the private key material inside a tamper resistant boundary so the key never exists in host memory. Signing is performed inside that boundary and only the signature leaves it. An attacker who fully controls the host can still ask the module to sign, but cannot extract the key, copy it, or use it offline against older traffic.

questions.explanation: The module value is containment of key material, not prevention of all misuse. Signatures come out, the key stays in, and a stolen host cannot export the key for later use.
questions.hint: Focus on what never leaves the device.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a hash collision costs and what finding one needs
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a duplicated digest as evidence about collision resistance

stimulus.body: The dome controller nightly file index is built by hashing each exposure name with a 160 bit digest. Two different exposures produced the same index value on the same night, and the index is used to look up records.

questions.stem: Given the log entry, what does the duplicated index value tell an attacker about the hashing scheme?

options.text: The hash function is broken for every input, so all records in the index can be forged.
options.misconception: overstates one collision into total breakage

options.text: A collision exists at that digest width, so a second record with the same index can be built.
The two exposures were identical files, so no collision was involved at all.
options.misconception: assumes duplicate inputs always explain duplicate outputs

options.text: The digest was computed with the wrong seed, so the collision reveals a setup mistake.
options.misconception: assumes collisions imply a wrong seed

questions.explanation: Two different inputs giving one output is a collision, which shows the digest width is too narrow for this index. It neither proves the function is broken for all inputs nor that the inputs were identical.
questions.hint: Ask what the attacker gained from two inputs sharing an output.

options.text: A slow salted password hash for the verifier, stored beside a per user random salt.
A fast keyed digest for the verifier, stored beside a per user random salt.
options.misconception: picks a fast digest for a value an attacker will try offline

options.text: A slow salted password hash for the verifier, stored with no salt at all in the table.
options.misconception: believes a slow hash alone removes the need for a salt

options.text: A fast keyed digest for the verifier, stored with no salt and reused across all accounts.
options.misconception: reuses one fast verifier across every account

questions.stem: Two record formats appear in the log. Format A signs the whole 40 kB observation record and carries a 512 byte signature. Format B signs only a 2 kB digest of that record and carries the same 512 byte signature. Which coverage statement follows?

options.text: Format A protects more fields, but Format B leaves the digest itself unprotected.
options.misconception: thinks the digest is unsigned in format B

options.text: Format B protects more fields, because a digest is a larger representation than the record.
options.misconception: assumes a digest covers more than its input

options.text: Both formats protect the same fields, since the signature length is identical in the two.
options.misconception: equates equal signature sizes with equal coverage

options.text: Format A covers every field of the record, while Format B covers the fields that were digested.

questions.explanation: A signature over a digest is only as good as what went into that digest. Format A authenticates all 40 kB directly, whereas Format B authenticates exactly the 2 kB that was hashed and nothing more.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a detached signature needs alongside it
questions.learningObjective: Explain the material a detached signature requires for verification
questions.stem: Explain what a detached signature needs beside the signature value itself before a verifier can accept the signed observation record.

answer.exemplar: A detached signature must travel with the digest of the exact bytes that were signed, plus the identity and key material needed to verify it. The verifier recomputes the digest of the received file, checks it against the supplied digest, and then checks the signature over that digest. Without the matching digest and the signer key the signature cannot be bound to the file.

questions.explanation: A signature binds a digest, so the verifier needs that digest and the signing key. The verifier recomputes the digest of the received bytes and confirms the signature covers the same value.
questions.hint: Ask what binds the signature to the file bytes.

options.misconception: assumes splitting removes all misuse risk

options.text: It replaces all hardware protection, because insiders can always be trusted.
options.misconception: believes insiders need no technical control

options.text: It lets any one shareholder unlock the key alone during an emergency.
options.misconception: confuses a threshold with a single holder scheme

options.text: It moves trust to a group, so no single person alone controls the key.

questions.explanation: A threshold scheme removes the single point of control: an attacker needs at least the threshold of colluding or compromised shareholders. Trust is redistributed among the group rather than concentrated.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a hash collision costs and what finding one needs
questions.learningObjective: Explain the work and the target of a collision search
questions.stem: Explain what it costs to find a collision in a truncated digest and what an attacker needs in order to succeed.

answer.exemplar: Finding a collision means producing two different records that produce the same truncated digest, and the attacker needs a second preimage for that digest rather than a preimage of the original record. The work scales with a birthday style search over the truncated width, so truncating a strong digest from 256 bits to 96 bits removes most of the protection while leaving the search feasible.

questions.explanation: A collision needs two different inputs with one output, so the attacker must build a second preimage for the digest. Truncating the output width cuts the work an attacker needs by roughly the square root of the bits removed.
questions.hint: Ask what must be produced, not just matched.

questions.learningObjective: State what a signature over a digest guarantees and does not guarantee

answer.exemplar: A signature over a digest guarantees that the holder of the signing key endorsed exactly the byte sequence that produced that digest, and that the digest was not altered afterward. questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a hash collision costs and what finding one needs
questions.learningObjective: Explain why truncation weakens collision resistance faster
questions.stem: Explain why truncating a strong digest weakens collision resistance faster than it weakens preimage resistance.

answer.exemplar: Preimage resistance requires about 2^n work for an n bit digest, while collision resistance requires about 2^(n/2) work. Truncating the digest from 256 bits to 96 bits therefore cuts collision work by a factor of about 2^80 while cutting preimage work by about 2^160. The shorter of the two bars is the one that determines how long the truncated digest stays safe, which is why truncation is so dangerous.

questions.explanation: Collision search costs about the square root of preimage search cost, so halving the digest width quarters the collision work but halves the preimage work. The weaker property is the one an index depends on.
questions.hint: Ask which property shrinks fastest.

options.misconception: signs metadata instead of the content

options.text: Sign the record length, then check that the length matches the stored file.

options.misconception: signs a label instead of the content

options.text: Sign a digest of the body, then recompute that digest and compare it.

options.text: A copy of the private key, so the verifier can re-derive the signature itself.
options.misconception: requires the private key at the verifier

options.text: A fresh certificate chain, so the verifier can confirm the issuer each time.
options.misconception: requires a full chain for every single check

options.text: The digest of the signed bytes, so the verifier can recompute and compare it.
The timestamp of signing, so the verifier can reject stale signatures.
options.misconception: believes a timestamp is the binding value

questions.explanation: The detached signature covers a digest, so the digest must travel with it or the verifier has nothing to bind the signature to. A private key or a timestamp would not supply that binding.

options.text: The status sources disagree, and the client trust rules decide which answer it believes.
The certificate is definitely revoked, because a single source saying so is conclusive.
options.misconception: treats one source as conclusive over a conflict

options.text: The certificate is definitely valid, because the majority of sources say it is good.
options.misconception: applies majority voting to status sources

options.text: The signature on answer B is broken, since it disagrees with the other answers.
options.misconception: infers a forged signature from disagreement alone

questions.explanation: Conflicting signed answers mean the sources are out of sync or one is stale, not that a signature is forged. Configured trust rules and answer freshness decide which one the client acts on.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: How a revoked status reaches a client
questions.learningObjective: Explain the exposure created by never checking revocation status
questions.stem: Explain why a client that never checks revocation status accepts a credential that an attacker has already invalidated.

answer.exemplar: A certificate proves only that a named issuer signed the public key at a stated time; it carries no statement about the key current standing. Without an active revocation check the client has no way to learn that the key was later invalidated, so it treats a stale but structurally valid credential as good. The window between invalidation and expiry is exactly the period an attacker wants.

questions.explanation: A certificate states that a key was issued, not that the key is still trusted today. Without a revocation lookup the client keeps accepting an invalidated credential for the window an attacker wants.
questions.hint: Ask what a certificate says about today.

options.misconception: treats a signing module as endpoint protection

options.misconception: confuses signing with encryption

options.misconception: assumes the module allows key sharing

options.text: Trust moves entirely to the shareholders, because the issuer is no longer involved.
options.misconception: claims the issuer drops out of the trust chain

options.text: Trust becomes collective, because rebuilding now needs several parties to act together.
Trust disappears, because an escrowed key can always be rebuilt by anyone.
options.misconception: believes escrow makes the key public

options.misconception: assumes the escrow service holds the shares

questions.topic: What a hash collision costs and what finding one needs
questions.learningObjective: Compare collision search work for two digest widths
questions.stem: Digest survey from the log: a 256 bit digest takes about 2^128 work to collide and about 2^256 work for a preimage, while a 64 bit digest takes about 2^32 and 2^64. How many times less collision work does the 64 bit digest need compared with the 256 bit digest?

options.text: About 2^96 times less, since 128 minus 32 is 96.
About 2^224 times less, since 256 minus 32 is 224.
options.misconception: subtracts the preimage exponents instead of the collision ones

options.text: About 2^32 times less, since the two digest widths differ by 32 bits.
options.misconception: uses the width difference instead of the exponent difference

options.text: About 2^128 times less, since the 256 bit digest always costs 2^128.
options.misconception: compares the wrong two exponents

questions.explanation: Collision work scales with half the digest width, so the 256 bit digest needs 2^128 and the 64 bit one needs 2^32. The ratio between them is 2^96.
questions.hint: Subtract the two collision exponents.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: How a password hash differs from a keyed digest
questions.learningObjective: Contrast a password hash with a keyed digest and their threats
questions.stem: Explain how a password hash differs from a keyed digest, and what attack the difference is designed to blunt.

answer.exemplar: A password hash is a one way, deliberately slow function of a password and a per user salt, and it is verified by re-hashing the candidate. A keyed digest is a fast, keyed function verified with the key and it is designed to be computed quickly, which is what makes signing and authenticating messages practical. The slow, salted choice exists so that an attacker who steals a verifier table cannot test candidate passwords at ordinary hashing speed.

questions.explanation: Password verifiers are attacked offline, so they are made slow and salted, while keyed digests are made fast because the key is assumed protected. Using a fast digest for stored passwords throws away the main defence.
questions.hint: Ask which side is assumed to be stolen.

options.misconception: pairs a long lifetime with an unreliable renewal path

options.text: Seven day validity, with renewal handled manually whenever a handshake fails.
options.misconception: pairs a short lifetime with manual renewal

One year validity, with renewal disabled because long lifetimes rarely expire.
options.misconception: assumes a long lifetime removes the need to renew

questions.stem: Handshake log for four client sessions: session 1 renewed at day 2, session 2 at day 9, session 3 at day 15, session 4 at day 30. Certificates are issued for 7 days. Which sessions used a certificate that expired while still in use?

options.text: Sessions 2 and 3, because they renewed after the seventh day of use.
options.misconception: reads the renewal times as certificate lifetimes

options.text: Sessions 2, 3 and 4, because each of them renewed after day 7.
Session 1 only, because it renewed on the second day of the trip.
options.misconception: finds only the first expiry instead of all of them

options.text: None of them, because renewal on any schedule keeps a certificate valid.
options.misconception: assumes renewal resets validity automatically

questions.explanation: A seven day certificate is good only for seven days from issuance, so a session still holding one after day 7 is at fault. Sessions 2, 3 and 4 all renewed later than that while session 1 renewed in time.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What boundary a hardware module draws
questions.learningObjective: Explain the module boundary and one attack it does not stop
questions.stem: Explain the boundary a hardware security module draws and name one attack it does not stop.

answer.exemplar: The module keeps private key material inside a tamper resistant boundary, performs key operations inside, and lets only results such as signatures leave. That stops an attacker who controls the host from reading, copying, or using the key offline. It does not stop a malicious or compromised host from asking the module to sign something it should not sign, because the module cannot judge the intent of its caller.

questions.explanation: The boundary contains key material against a hostile host, so key theft by reading memory or files is blocked. Intent based misuse, where the host simply asks for a signature it should not have, is not blocked.
questions.hint: Ask what the module cannot judge.

questions.learningObjective: State the checks a verifier performs on a detached signature
questions.stem: A detached signature is verified against a digest supplied separately from the signature. What must the verifier check for the check to mean anything?

options.text: That the digest was computed with the private key, so it cannot be forged.
options.misconception: imposes an impossible check on a public digest

options.text: That the digest is longer than the signature, so the signature has room to fit.
options.misconception: confuses length with correctness of binding

options.text: That the recomputed digest matches the supplied one and the signature covers it.
That the digest was signed recently, so old bundles are rejected on time alone.
options.misconception: relies on age instead of binding

questions.explanation: Verification means recomputing the digest of the received bytes, comparing it with the detached value, and checking the signature over that value. Anything else leaves the signature attached to nothing.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a detached signature needs alongside it
questions.learningObjective: Explain the material a detached bundle needs and who must compute it
questions.stem: Explain what a detached signature must carry alongside it, and why the supplier of the record cannot be trusted to supply that item alone.

answer.exemplar: A detached signature must carry the digest of the bytes that were signed and identify the key that produced it, so the verifier can recompute the digest and check the signature. The digest cannot simply be taken on trust from whoever supplies the bundle, because the verifier must confirm that the digest describes the actual bytes it received rather than bytes the signer never saw and that an attacker chose.

questions.explanation: The bundle needs the signed digest and an identifiable key, and the verifier must recompute the digest itself rather than accept a supplied one. Otherwise the signature could be bound to content the signer never saw.
questions.hint: Ask why the digest must be recomputed.

questions.topic: What short-lived certificates demand in return
questions.learningObjective: Count renewals made within a set head start of expiry
questions.stem: Renewal schedule: the site certificate is issued for 30 days. Renewals in the log happened on day 10, day 33, day 50 and day 74. How many renewals happened less than 11 days before the certificate in use expired?

options.text: None of them, because every renewal in the log came at least 12 days early.
options.misconception: reads every gap as large

options.text: Two of them, the renewals on day 33 and day 74.
Three of them, because only the first renewal was made with plenty of notice.
options.misconception: miscounts the qualifying renewals

options.text: All four of them, because the 30 day lifetime always makes a renewal early.
options.misconception: ignores the actual renewal dates

questions.explanation: Each head start is the gap between the renewal day and the expiry of the certificate it replaced. Those gaps are 20, 7, 13 and 6 days, so only the 7 day and 6 day gaps fall below 11.
questions.hint: Compute the gap before each previous expiry.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What boundary a hardware module draws
questions.learningObjective: Interpret module activity logs as evidence of containment
questions.stem: Module activity log: signing operations 1240, key export attempts 12, export attempts that returned key material 0. What does the log show about the boundary the module drew?

options.text: The module was penetrated, since export attempts prove key material left it.
options.misconception: treats attempts as successful exports

options.text: The boundary held, since none of the export attempts returned any key material.
The module was never attacked, because export attempts are not recorded.
options.misconception: reads a recorded attempt as no attempt

options.text: The boundary held, because 1240 signings show the key was working normally.
options.misconception: treats normal use as proof of containment

questions.explanation: The boundary is demonstrated by outcomes, not by the absence of attempts. Twelve export attempts were made and all twelve returned nothing, so the key never left.
questions.hint: Ask what the outcomes of the attempts show.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a threshold escrow changes about trust
questions.learningObjective: Explain the trust change produced by threshold escrow
questions.stem: Explain what a threshold escrow changes about trust when a signing key is split among several shareholders.

answer.exemplar: A threshold escrow splits a key into shares so that any set at or above the threshold can rebuild it and no smaller set can. The trust change is structural: a single compromised or coerced shareholder is no longer enough, because an attacker or insider needs several parties to act together and no holder can be pressured alone. The scheme does not make the key unconditionally safe, since colluding holders can still rebuild it together.

questions.explanation: Splitting the key removes single party control: an attacker needs the threshold, not one holder. It does not remove the risk entirely, since colluding shareholders can still rebuild the key together.
questions.hint: Ask how many parties an attacker now needs.
